extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical literature, literary critics, and philosophers of art (readers of Aristotle's Poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and critical commentary on Aristotle’s theory of poetry and fine art (the Poetics): sets out aesthetic principles for composing and judging poetry, tragedy, comedy, and other fine arts, with textual notes and examples from Greek literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the defining aesthetic term
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Imitation’ as the common characteristic of the Fine Arts: a current phrase interpreted anew by Aristotle; the objects of aesthetic imitation are human Character, Emotion, Action (ἤθη, πάθη, πράξεις).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work of Art is a likeness (ὁμοίωμα) of an original, not a symbolical representation (σημεῖον). A work reproduces its original not as it is in itself, but as presented to the phantasy (φαντασία). Different arts imitate in different senses (music, painting, dancing, poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as expression of the universal (τὸ καθόλου)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry, in its highest manifestation, is an expression of the universal element in human life; it is an idealised image of human life—character, emotion, action—under sensuous forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception distinguishes poetry from mere factual reporting: the poet represents what is generally true or possible rather than particular empirical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Fine Art and Useful Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The theoretic distinction between Fine and Useful Art first established by Aristotle; 'Art imitates Nature' is specially applied to Useful Art, which follows Nature’s methods and supplies her defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful arts imitate Nature's productive ends; fine arts imitate human life and universals. When evaluating works, note whether the art's purpose is utility or aesthetic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs. historical truth (probability and possibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is not a reproduction of empirical fact: it records probabilities and possibilities; poetry excludes the rule of Chance and represents what is plausible or necessary in human actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem should present internally plausible sequences (probable impossibilities are acceptable if they cohere poetically). The poet aims at the 'general idea' rather than mere reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of Fine Art: pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Fine Art is pleasure: lower forms afford pastime (παιδιά), higher forms give noble enjoyment (διαγωγή) akin to supreme happiness (εὐδαιμονία).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works by the kind and quality of pleasure they provide to the spectator/reader; fine art aims at higher, contemplative pleasure rather than simple diversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure of the spectator as primary end
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of the hearer or spectator (θεατής) is regarded as the end of Art in Aristotle’s account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a work, give weight to its effect on the audience and the nature of enjoyment it produces (playful, moral, contemplative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of aesthetic and moral functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes the educational (moral) from the aesthetic function of Poetry: his critical estimates rest on purely aesthetic grounds, though some rules imply moral seriousness (e.g., tragic characters must be σπουδαῖοι).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should primarily address aesthetic success (form, unity, effect), while acknowledging that some formal requirements have moral implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and function of Tragedy (purpose: katharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is defined in terms of producing katharsis of pity and fear; the tragic katharsis involves an emotional relief and clarification of emotion (medical metaphor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tragic works by how effectively they arouse and purify pity and fear, and whether the process clarifies emotions rather than merely shocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for cathartic treatment of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Catharsis is possible only under certain conditions (the representation must be ordered and not merely chaotic); the process is connected with the representation of universals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the sequence of events, character portrayal, and dramatic devices enable the spectator to experience and be clarified by emotions, rather than being confused or numbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action as primary dramatic unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Action is the primary unity: tragedy should be an organic whole with a beginning, middle, and end; the law of unity applies to epic and drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the plot constitutes a single, coherent action where each part is necessary to the whole; subsidiary unities (time, place) are subordinate to unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (μῦθος) as the ‘soul’ and primary element of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot or Action is the primary element according to Aristotle: action is privileged over character; the intimate relation between action and character must, however, be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a tragedy first by the construction and necessity of its events (reversals, recognitions, causal sequence); then by how character supports and is manifested through action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure devices: reversal (περιπέτεια) and recognition (ἀναγνώρισις)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of the situation (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis) are central devices producing dramatic effect and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the timing, inevitability, and emotional impact of reversals and recognitions—whether they arise naturally from the plot and heighten catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic hero and the notion of hamartia
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s ideal protagonist (ch. xiii.) is derived from the function of tragedy to produce pity and fear; excluded types include blameless goodness and manifest villainy; the tragic flaw (ἁμαρτία) is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a hero, consider whether they are great/spoudaios with a fall understandable through hamartia, enabling pity and fear, rather than being simply virtuous or villainous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ἦθος) and thought (διάνοια) as components of dramatic personae
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethos and Dianoia constitute character in the largest sense; Aristotle subordinates character to action but insists on their intimate relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters for ethical plausibility and intelligence (dianoia) insofar as they motivate and are revealed by actions; modern drama places more stress on delineation of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation and generalisation across genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts idealise in different senses; tragedy and comedy each idealise life (tragedy via idealised persons, comedy via personified ideals and generalisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work achieves an appropriate level of idealisation—representing general truths without losing dramatic plausibility or individual interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s universalising power
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy creates personified ideals and exhibits a generalising power which operates differently from tragedy’s idealisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge comedic works by their capacity to generalise character-types, the effectiveness of names and comic devices, and the balance between humour and pathos where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic medium: verse, rhythm, music, and other elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse and rhythm are elements of poetry; music, dance, metre, and rhythm contribute to the medium of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poetic works, consider formal elements (metre, rhythm, music) and how they serve imitation and the expression of the universal; assess whether form enhances or distracts from content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic possibility: allowable improbabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic ‘probabilities’ differ from empirical probabilities; 'probable impossibilities' are acceptable in poetry provided they cohere poetically and serve the general idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for fictional liberties that convey general truths; penalize inventions that break internal plausibility or serve no poetic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic semblance (aesthetic semblance) over literal copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle rejects the view that imitation is literal copying; aesthetic semblance emphasises presenting the universal as it appears to the imagination, not a facsimile of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fidelity to human universals and the convincingness of representation rather than strict realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation of time and place (treatment of temporal/spatial unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle notes practices about 'unity of time' (single revolution of the sun) and does not mention 'unity of place'; time and place are idealised and subordinate to unity of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dramatic time/place for their contribution to unity of action; do not enforce artificial exactness of clock-time if it undermines the plot’s organic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of poetic recognition and ‘poetic justice’
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition and reversal culminate in a form of poetic justice and contribute to the pleasure of tragedy; poetry represents universal moral patterns rather than didactic prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether resolutions produce intelligible moral patterns that cohere with the universal represented—avoid conflating poetic justice with moral didacticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of minor rules to artistic truth (tentativeness of rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of Aristotle’s rules are tentative rather than dogmatic; some rules (e.g., requisites for tragic protagonists) may need revision to accommodate great works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply formal rules flexibly: use them as critical heuristics rather than absolute prescriptions; consider historical practices and exemplary countercases (e.g., Antigone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of ancient vs modern emphasis (plot vs character balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle claims ancient drama emphasised plot over character; modern drama increasingly stresses character delineation—both approaches valid but must maintain unity and organic coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging works across periods, take genre-historical expectations into account: measure success relative to the aims and conventions of the form.
